title: Stand Fast
author: Tom Bennett
summary: Bennett answers a TES piece that used his work as the Department for Education's behaviour adviser as evidence that English school behaviour has deteriorated, and he answers it as a statistics argument rather than a reputational one. His first move is to show that the survey comparison at the heart of the critique is invalid, because the earlier 75 percent figure pooled classroom teachers with senior leaders while the later 46 percent figure counted teachers alone, and leaders reliably rate behaviour more favourably. He then attacks the use of suspension and exclusion rates as an outcome measure at all, arguing they record how adults responded rather than how children behaved, much as arrest figures record policing rather than crime. A 63 percent rise in permanent exclusions, he notes, is a shift from ten to thirteen students per ten thousand. He also rejects the premise that he controls English schools, then offers the Behaviour Hubs programme as the actual test case, citing its independent evaluation and Ofsted movement among graduating schools. The piece closes on his substantive position, that children need both love and structure, high regard and high standards, and that teachers themselves name consistency as what produces good behaviour.
points: Shows the headline survey comparison is invalid because one sample included a senior-leader booster and the other did not, a problem the NFER researchers had already flagged themselves.
Argues exclusion and suspension figures measure institutional response rather than pupil conduct, so a rising rate can indicate a system recovering rather than deteriorating.
Reframes the 63 percent rise in permanent exclusions as a move from 10 to 13 students per 10,000, and sets it against weapons incidents and 63,000 suspensions for attacks on staff.

Points to Behaviour Hubs as the only defensible test of his approach, noting the independent evaluation found strong evidence that pupil behaviour improved and that Ofsted grades shifted sharply among graduating schools.
Dismisses the student satisfaction data used against the programme as unweighted, uncontrolled and drawn from different cohorts across the lockdown period.
quotes: But it’s wrong. The 75% figure included both classroom teachers and senior leaders. The 46% figure is teachers alone. And we know that leaders consistently rate behaviour more positively than classroom teachers in most surveys.
This is comparing apples with elephants. These are different surveys and different respondents.

But suspension/ exclusion rates aren’t a way to evaluate behaviour; they are a record of how we’ve responded to behaviour. If arrests for burglaries went up, it doesn’t mean that there are more burglaries; it could just mean that police were getting better at catching burglars.
In 2023/24 permanent exclusions were at 0.13%, or 13 students on 10,000. In 2010 the rate was 0.1%, or 10 students in every 10,000. A rise in 3 students for every 10,000 students.
Despite what some terminally online people think, I’m not actually in charge of every school in England. I advise the Department. England didn’t suddenly switch over to the methods I advocate.
We do! The independent final evaluation of Behaviour Hubs concluded that the programme ‘largely achieved its objectives’.
The OECD reports that ‘disciplinary climate in UK science lessons improved between 2015 and 2025’. Which is almost exactly the period supposedly represented by the deterioration narrative.

Kids need love, and they need structure. They need pathways to succeed behaviourally, they need to know how to navigate a complex social world, and they need to know where the boundaries are. They need high regard and high standards. If you get that right, everything else is possible.
